name: THE DEEP BLUE BRIE BURGER (comes with blue cheese and brie)

recipe.history:
Blue cheese and Brie represent two of the most celebrated and historically rich traditions in French and European cheesemaking, and placing them together on a single burger is an act of audacious generosity that rewards both the daring and the devoted. Brie takes its name from the Brie region of France, east of Paris, where it has been produced since at least the eighth century CE — the Frankish king Charlemagne reportedly tasted it at the abbey of Reuil-en-Brie in 774 and was so impressed that he ordered two loads sent to him in Aix-la-Chapelle every year. The cheese's distinctive white bloomy rind, produced by the Penicillium camemberti mold, develops within days of the cheese's formation and gives the paste beneath it a soft, runny, buttery interior when ripe, with flavors of mushroom, cream, and fresh grass that become more earthy and pungent with age. Brie de Meaux and Brie de Melun are the two varieties granted Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) status in France. Blue cheese — in its French form Roquefort, made from sheep's milk aged in the limestone caves of Combalou near the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon — is even older, with legend crediting its discovery to a young shepherd who left his lunch (bread and fresh ewes' milk curd) in a cave and returned months later to find it transformed by mold into something extraordinary. Roquefort is protected by law and labeled with a red sheep logo; only cheese made from the milk of Lacaune sheep, from specific geographic areas, and aged in the natural Combalou caves qualifies. Beyond Roquefort, blue cheese traditions flourished across Europe — Gorgonzola in Italy (dating to the ninth century), Stilton in England (eighteenth century), Danish Blue in Denmark (twentieth century) — each regional tradition developing its own bacterial and mold cultures, its own characteristic balance of salt, fat, and intense blue flavor.

Blue cheese and Brie arrived in American burger culture through distinctly different paths that converge at the premium end of the burger spectrum. Blue cheese crumbles became a standard upscale burger topping in the 1980s and 1990s, when American steakhouses began translating the classic steak bleu pairing to burgers — the logic being that if blue cheese complemented the mineral richness of a rare ribeye, it would do the same for a beef patty cooked to the same temperature. Brie on a burger is a more recent and more dramatic development, requiring chefs to either slice and melt the cheese on the patty or serve it at room temperature as a spread — since properly ripe Brie at room temperature is already almost liquid and needs no heat to soften. The combination of both cheeses — blue cheese's saltiness, sharpness, and intensity alongside Brie's creaminess, earthiness, and mild sweetness — creates a flavor complexity that no single cheese can match, the two extremes of the French cheese tradition meeting on a beef patty.

I once spent a week in Paris eating nothing but baguettes, runny Brie, and Roquefort, and I came home convinced that French cheese culture represents one of humanity's highest culinary achievements. Two weeks later I put Brie and Roquefort on a burger together to see what would happen. What happened was that the sharp, salty, funk-forward Roquefort cut through the creaminess of the Brie in exactly the way a squeeze of lemon cuts through the richness of butter — not competing with it but defining it, making the creaminess more perceptible by contrasting against it. The medium-rare patty beneath them was the sea they both floated on: rich, beefy, and assertive enough to prevent either cheese from dominating entirely. I served it to my neighbor who had declared himself indifferent to cheese. He ate two. He remains my friend.

Two of the world's great cheeses deserve the best possible beef beneath them, and the best possible beef is a patty cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit without exception or negotiation. Brie melts and flows at this temperature when placed on a hot patty. Blue cheese softens and becomes creamier, its sharp edges rounded slightly by the warmth without losing the funky, assertive quality that defines it. A well-done patty provides neither the heat nor the juiciness that allows these transformations to happen correctly — it is too dry, too compact, and too neutral to serve as the foundation that both cheeses require. At medium rare, the beef is confident, the Brie is flowing, the blue cheese is bold, and the three together create something that justifies every extravagance involved in their creation.
ingredients: 115g Roquefort or quality Gorgonzola, crumbled into small pieces
1 tbsp heavy cream (to loosen slightly for spreading)
200g ripe Brie, rind removed (or left on, per preference), cut into 1/4-inch slices
For the red wine onion jam:
salt and black pepper to taste
1 large pear or apple, thinly sliced (optional but exceptional)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes. Rise in oiled bowl 1 hour. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

2. Make the red wine onion jam: Heat butter and olive oil in a heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add sliced red onions and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring often, for 20–25 minutes until deeply softened, golden, and beginning to caramelize. Add sugar, thyme, red wine, red wine vinegar. Stir and simmer on medium-low heat for 10–15 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and the mixture is thick, jammy, and deeply flavored. Season with salt and pepper. Cool slightly.

3. Make the walnut-honey mustard: Toast walnuts in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3–4 minutes until fragrant. Cool and chop finely. Whisk together Dijon mustard, honey, walnuts, and red wine vinegar. Season with salt. Refrigerate.
4. Prepare the blue cheese: In a small bowl, combine crumbled blue cheese with heavy cream. Gently fold together until slightly creamy but still textured. Set aside at room temperature.

5. Prepare the Brie: Remove Brie from the refrigerator 30 minutes before cooking to allow it to come close to room temperature, which will allow it to melt more readily when placed on the hot patty. Slice or portion into enough pieces to cover each patty.

6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes to build a crust. Flip once. Immediately lay Brie slices over each patty, covering the surface. Crumble blue cheese over the Brie. Tent loosely with foil to encourage the Brie to begin melting and the blue cheese to warm and soften. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes off heat.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread walnut-honey mustard on both bun halves. Spoon a generous layer of red wine onion jam on the bottom bun. Place the double-cheese-topped, medium-rare patty on the onion jam. The Brie should be partially melted and running slightly; the blue cheese should be warm and creamy. Add thin slices of pear or apple over the cheese if using — the fruit's sweetness is extraordinary against the blue cheese. Add a small handful of baby arugula. Finish with a few fresh thyme leaves and a pinch of flaky sea salt over the top. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately.
